title.en: Section 1 - A conversation about joining a sports club

sections.passage: A conversation between a receptionist, Lisa, and a new member, Michael, who wants to join the Riverside Sports and Fitness Club. Michael has recently moved to the area and is looking for a gym that offers a variety of activities. Lisa explains that the club has three membership categories: Standard, Premium, and VIP. The Standard membership costs 45 pounds per month and includes access to the gym, swimming pool, and group fitness classes. The Premium membership costs 75 pounds per month and adds access to the tennis courts, squash courts, and sauna facilities. The VIP membership costs 120 pounds per month and includes everything plus personal training sessions and priority booking for all facilities. Michael is interested in the Premium membership because he enjoys playing tennis. Lisa mentions that there is currently a special offer where new members receive the first month free if they sign a twelve-month contract. Michael asks about the opening hours, and Lisa tells him the gym is open from 5:30 AM to 10:30 PM on weekdays and 7:00 AM to 9:00 PM on weekends. She also mentions that the swimming pool has separate times for lane swimming and casual swimming. Michael needs to complete a health questionnaire and provide a passport-sized photograph for his membership card. Lisa offers to show him around the facilities that afternoon, and Michael agrees to come back at 3 PM.

title.en: Section 2 - A guided tour of a historical building
title.zh: 第二部分 - 历史建筑的导览参观

sections.passage: A tour guide, Margaret, is leading a group of visitors through Whitmore Manor, a historic country house that was built in 1685. The house was originally owned by the Whitmore family, who were wealthy landowners and prominent members of the local community for over three centuries. The main house contains 42 rooms, including a grand ballroom, a library with over 15,000 books, and a chapel that was added in 1720. The gardens, which cover approximately 12 acres, were designed by the famous landscape architect Capability Brown in 1762. Margaret explains that the house was donated to the National Trust in 1953 by the last surviving member of the Whitmore family, Sir Edward Whitmore, who had no children. Since then, the house has undergone extensive restoration work, costing over 3 million pounds. The most recent restoration project, completed in 2019, focused on the east wing, which had suffered significant water damage. Visitors can see the original 17th-century kitchen, which has been preserved with its large stone fireplace and copper cooking pots. The first floor contains the family bedrooms, each decorated in a different historical period, from the Stuart era to the Victorian age. Margaret points out a particularly valuable painting by Thomas Gainsborough, which hangs in the drawing room and is estimated to be worth over 2 million pounds. Photography is allowed in the gardens but not inside the house. The tour concludes at the gift shop, where visitors can purchase souvenirs and locally produced goods.

title.en: Section 3 - Two students discussing a research project
title.zh: 第三部分 - 两名学生讨论研究项目

sections.passage: Two students, Sophie and Ryan, are discussing their research project on the effectiveness of different study techniques. They are required to design and conduct an experiment for their Psychology course. Sophie suggests investigating the testing effect, which is the finding that practising retrieval of information from memory is more effective for long-term retention than simply re-reading notes. Ryan agrees and proposes comparing three study methods: re-reading notes, completing practice tests, and teaching the material to someone else. They plan to recruit 60 participants from their university, dividing them into three groups of 20. Each group will study the same material on the topic of cognitive psychology using their assigned method for one week. After the study period, all participants will take the same test to measure their retention. Sophie wants to use multiple-choice questions for the test because they are easier to score objectively. Ryan argues that a combination of multiple-choice and short-answer questions would provide a more comprehensive assessment. They compromise by using both question types. They need to submit their research proposal to their supervisor, Dr. Patterson, by the end of next week. Sophie mentions that she has found several relevant academic papers, including a meta-analysis published in Psychological Bulletin that examined over 200 studies on the testing effect. Ryan suggests they should also include a control group that receives no study materials, but Sophie points out that this would be unethical as it could disadvantage those participants in their actual coursework. They decide to present their preliminary findings at the departmental research conference in March.

title.en: Section 4 - A lecture on marine biology
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于海洋生物学的讲座

sections.passage: A university lecture by Dr. Helen Foster on the topic of coral reef ecosystems and the threats they face. Dr. Foster begins by explaining that coral reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth, supporting approximately 25 percent of all marine species despite covering less than 1 percent of the ocean floor. She describes the symbiotic relationship between coral polyps and zooxanthellae, microscopic algae that live within the coral tissue and provide up to 90 percent of the coral's energy through photosynthesis. In return, the coral provides the algae with shelter and the compounds they need for photosynthesis. The lecture then focuses on coral bleaching, which occurs when environmental stress, primarily rising sea temperatures, causes corals to expel their zooxanthellae. Without these algae, the coral turns white and, if the stress continues for more than about four to eight weeks, the coral dies. Dr. Foster presents data showing that global sea surface temperatures have risen by approximately 0.9 degrees Celsius since 1900, and that mass bleaching events have become five times more frequent since 1980. The Great Barrier Reef in Australia has experienced three major bleaching events in the last five years alone. She also discusses ocean acidification, which is caused by the ocean absorbing excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. As the ocean becomes more acidic, it becomes harder for corals to build their calcium carbonate skeletons. Dr. Foster estimates that ocean acidity has increased by approximately 30 percent since the Industrial Revolution. She concludes by presenting several conservation strategies, including the establishment of marine protected areas, the development of heat-resistant coral strains through selective breeding, and the use of artificial reef structures to provide new habitats for marine organisms.

title.en: Passage 1 - The Life Cycle of Salmon
title.zh: 文章1 - 鲑鱼的生命周期

sections.passage: Salmon are among the most remarkable creatures in the natural world, known for their extraordinary ability to navigate thousands of miles across open ocean and return to the exact river where they were born to spawn and die. This journey, known as the salmon run, is one of nature's most dramatic events. The life cycle of a salmon begins when a female deposits her eggs, known as roe, in a shallow depression called a redd, which she has excavated in the gravel bed of a freshwater stream. A single female can lay between 2,500 and 7,000 eggs depending on the species. After the male fertilises the eggs, the female covers them with gravel to protect them from predators. The eggs incubate for several months, typically hatching in the spring when water temperatures begin to rise. The newly hatched salmon, called alevins, carry a yolk sac attached to their bodies that provides nourishment for the first few weeks of life. Once the yolk sac is absorbed, the young salmon, now called fry, begin to feed independently on insects and small invertebrates. Over the following months, the fry develop into parr, identifiable by the distinctive dark vertical bars on their sides. Parr typically spend one to three years in freshwater before undergoing a dramatic physiological transformation known as smoltification. During this process, their bodies adapt to life in salt water by producing special proteins that help regulate the balance of salt and water in their cells. The young salmon, now called smolts, migrate downstream to the ocean, where they will spend between one and five years feeding and growing to adult size. In the ocean, salmon feed voraciously on smaller fish, squid, and crustaceans, growing rapidly and accumulating the energy reserves they will need for their return journey. When the time comes to spawn, adult salmon stop eating entirely and begin their upstream migration, often travelling hundreds of miles and leaping up waterfalls to reach their natal stream. After spawning, most Pacific salmon species die within a few days, their bodies providing essential nutrients to the surrounding ecosystem. Atlantic salmon, however, can survive to spawn multiple times.

title.en: Passage 2 - The History of the London Underground
title.zh: 文章2 - 伦敦地铁的历史

sections.passage: The London Underground, affectionately known as the Tube, is the world's oldest underground railway system. Its first section, the Metropolitan Railway, opened on 10 January 1863, running between Paddington and Farringdon Street. The idea for an underground railway had been proposed as early as the 1830s, as London's streets were becoming increasingly congested with horse-drawn carriages, omnibuses, and pedestrians. Charles Pearson, a solicitor and campaigner, was one of the earliest advocates for underground rail travel and played a crucial role in promoting the concept. The original Metropolitan Railway used gas-lit wooden carriages hauled by steam locomotives. Despite initial concerns about ventilation and safety, the railway proved enormously popular, carrying 38,000 passengers on its opening day. The success of the Metropolitan Railway led to the construction of additional underground lines. The District Railway, which later became the District line, opened in 1868, connecting the western and southern parts of central London. The development of electric traction in the 1890s revolutionised underground travel, eliminating the smoke and steam that had plagued earlier lines. The City and South London Railway, which opened in 1890, was the world's first deep-level electric railway. The iconic Tube map, which has become one of the most recognisable designs in the world, was created in 1931 by Harry Beck, an engineering draftsman who worked for London Transport. Beck's revolutionary design abandoned geographical accuracy in favour of a simplified schematic diagram that used only horizontal, vertical, and 45-degree lines. His design was initially rejected by London Transport's management as too radical, but after a successful trial run as a pocket map in 1933, it was quickly adopted as the standard. Today, the London Underground serves 272 stations across 11 lines, carrying approximately 5 million passenger journeys per day. The system covers 402 kilometres of track, making it one of the most extensive metro networks in the world.

sections.passage: Sleep is one of the most fundamental biological processes, yet for centuries it was largely misunderstood and undervalued by scientists. It was not until the invention of the electroencephalogram in the 1920s that researchers were able to measure brain activity during sleep and discover that the sleeping brain is far from inactive. We now know that sleep is a complex, dynamic process that plays a critical role in physical health, cognitive function, and emotional regulation. Human sleep is divided into two main types: non-rapid eye movement sleep and rapid eye movement sleep. NREM sleep is further divided into three stages, each progressively deeper. Stage 1 is a light transitional phase between wakefulness and sleep, lasting only a few minutes. Stage 2 is a deeper form of sleep, during which heart rate and body temperature decrease and the brain produces characteristic bursts of activity called sleep spindles. Stage 3, also known as slow-wave sleep or deep sleep, is the most restorative phase, during which the body repairs tissues, strengthens the immune system, and consolidates declarative memories, which are facts and events. REM sleep, which was first identified by researchers at the University of Chicago in 1953, is characterised by rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, and near-complete muscle paralysis. During REM sleep, the brain is almost as active as during waking hours, and this phase is believed to be essential for emotional processing and the consolidation of procedural memories, which are skills and habits. Adults typically cycle through all stages of sleep four to six times per night, with each cycle lasting approximately 90 minutes. The proportion of time spent in each stage changes throughout the night, with more deep sleep occurring in the first half and more REM sleep in the second half. Chronic sleep deprivation, defined as regularly getting fewer than seven hours of sleep per night, has been linked to a wide range of health problems, including obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and weakened immune function. Research has also shown that even one night of poor sleep can impair cognitive performance to a degree comparable to alcohol intoxication.

prompt.en: Some people believe that allowing children to make their own choices on everyday matters such as food, clothes, and entertainment is likely to result in a society of individuals who only think about their own wishes.
